patterns_data.top_pattern: TX acute hospital volume surge in HMO and POS
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual acute hospital spend in TX HMO and POS
patterns_data.pattern_details: TX is the clearest broad utilization story in the analysis. Acute hospital spend rose sharply in both HMO and POS because claim volume increased, while paid per admission fell in both products. This points to a utilization and admission-management issue first, not a broad unit-cost escalation.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: This is the single largest cost driver and will not be offset by smaller pricing or coding fixes elsewhere.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Start a TX acute inpatient authorization and admission-management workplan for HMO and POS, focused on preventable admits, level-of-care review, and redirecting avoidable cases to lower-cost settings where appropriate.
evidence_summary: TX HMO acute hospital spend increased by $9.8M on 2,373 more claims, while paid per admit fell by about $678.
TX POS acute hospital spend increased by $5.5M on 1,472 more claims, while paid per admit fell by about $495.
These two TX acute hospital product lines account for more than 80% of the identified positive delta in the top operational findings.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Not Mapped buckets are masking real provider and authorization signals
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Facility and clinical classification across CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED
patterns_data.pattern_details: A material share of the increase sits in Not Mapped facility or clinical buckets, so teams cannot reliably tell whether the issue is utilization, provider mix, or classification error. The biggest examples include Orange County Global Medical Center in CA, outpatient drug cases in UNATTRIBUTED, and CORAM CVS Specialty Infusion Services in CO. This is a gating validation pattern: mapping and coding should be corrected before the confirmed claims are reassigned to UM, network, or clinical workflows.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: If unmapped claims are not fixed first, the organization risks chasing false provider or authorization trends.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a targeted mapping and coding correction pass for Not Mapped facility and outpatient clinical buckets in CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED, then reclassify confirmed claims into the proper operational and clinical review queues.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Not Mapped facility and clinical buckets are materially contributing to the increase across multiple segments and providers, so attribution is not reliable enough for direct action without correction.
evidence_summary: CA HMO Not Mapped facility claims at Orange County Global Medical Center added $427K from 1 claim.
UNATTRIBUTED OP Mgmt Oth Misc / Not Mapped / Drugs added $328K from 2 claims.
CO HMO Not Mapped facility claims at CORAM CVS Specialty Infusion Services added $78K from 3 claims.
CA EPO Not Mapped facility claims tied to Stephen L Hofkin added $36K despite 1 fewer claim.

patterns_data.top_pattern: ME, NH, and OH HMO acute spend is concentrated in a few very expensive admissions
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual HMO acute hospital and IP Med/Surg spend in ME, NH, and OH
patterns_data.pattern_details: This is a low-volume outlier pattern, not broad-based acute hospital growth. A single ME transplant-sized admission, NH back-problem admissions, and concentrated OH exposure at Euclid Hospital are driving most of the increase. Because only a small number of cases are responsible for a seven-figure change, case-level clinical and payment review is the right action.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: A handful of high-cost acute stays can distort market trends and often require different action than broad utilization growth.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Perform case-level clinical and reimbursement review for the ME, NH, and OH HMO acute admissions, focusing on transplant severity, back-problem inpatient necessity, and provider-specific pricing at Euclid Hospital.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The impact is concentrated in very few admissions with low-baseline and small-count flags, so confirmation is needed before broader policy action.
evidence_summary: A single ME HMO acute admission tied to liver transplant drove $486K.
NH IP Med/Surg back-problem cases under Medical Back Problems with MCC added $423K across 4 claims.
OH HMO acute spend at Euclid Hospital added $79K across 33 claims with higher paid per claim.

patterns_data.top_pattern: ME PPO spend is shifting into rehab and unattributed facility claims
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual PPO non-acute facility spend in ME
patterns_data.pattern_details: ME PPO growth is occurring outside acute hospital settings, split between physical rehab and claims without usable facility mapping. Volume is the main driver in both areas, which suggests a possible site-of-care shift into post-acute or other non-acute settings. Because part of the pattern sits in Not Mapped facilities, mapping should be corrected before utilization policy is changed.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Non-acute migration can create a durable spend shift if it is not distinguished from simple facility classification problems.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Validate ME PPO facility mapping first, then review physical rehab referral and authorization patterns to determine whether post-acute utilization controls need to be tightened.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Part of the increase is in Not Mapped facility claims, so the site-of-care story is not fully reliable until facility attribution is corrected.
evidence_summary: ME PPO Not Mapped facility claims added $158K on 60 more claims, with lower paid per claim.
ME PPO Physical Rehab added $134K on 48 more claims, with about $2.6K higher paid per claim.
